title: Pivot Scoop
family: Pivoting roller scoop with direct receiver pickup
summary: Capture one crosswise coral at the floor, rotate the whole scoop, and let the receiver take it directly without a separate conveyor.
advantage: The same scoop captures and carries the piece; a low inner pivot avoids a tall fixed receiver tower.
risk: Coral may fall from the rotating scoop. Retention, dogleg arm clearance and the receiver grip are unverified.
firstTest: Rotate a cardboard scoop around the proposed pivot with one pipe and a full bumper block; test retention and direct receiver access.
inspiration: Independent pivot-scoop hypothesis for the team shop; not a reproduction of a team's geometry.

title: Rising Drawer
family: Translating pickup drawer with captive cam rise
summary: Extend a rolling drawer nose to the floor, capture crosswise coral, then retract along a rising cam before translating above the bumper.
advantage: Translation preserves crosswise orientation and reaches a rearward receiver without swinging the entire intake through a large arc.
risk: The captive rise cam is the major complexity. Follower binding, required drive force, drawer sag and full stow are unverified.
firstTest: Slide a flat-stock drawer through a cardboard cam track beside an intact bumper block; check nose rise, binding and pipe retention.
inspiration: Independent cam-guided drawer hypothesis using router-cut tracks and flat stock; not a team geometry copy.

title: Tip Cradle
family: Powered roller capture cradle with tip-and-discharge handoff
summary: Roll nose-in coral up a sloped cradle, hold one piece, then tip the cradle and power it into a separate lengthwise receiver.
advantage: Powered capture and discharge are separate from the short tipping motion; the receiver stays inboard at a distinct lengthwise offer pose.
risk: Retention and discharge gating are unclear. Coral may escape while tipping or double-feed; nose-in entry is assumed, not 360-degree yaw acceptance.
firstTest: Use a tilting plywood cradle and two rubber rolls to capture one nose-in pipe; stop, tip and discharge while checking escape and release timing.
inspiration: Independent powered tipping-cradle hypothesis using flat side plates; no claim to reproduce a team's geometry.
